archetype.name: Better Than Its Record (special-teams sunk)
archetype.definition: A team that plays roughly even hockey at 5-on-5 and defends its own end well, but whose penalty kill, goaltending and luck in close games have turned a break-even process into a bottom-four record.

report.headline: An even-strength .500 team buried by a broken kill and leaky goaltending
report.take:
Los Angeles sits seventh in the Pacific at 7-12-2, 29th of 32 on the site, and on a pace for 62 standings points. That is a lottery team's résumé. The 5-on-5 numbers say something different. The Kings hold 50.4% of expected goals (15th) and 50.0% of shot attempts (16th). They also hold opposing centers to fewer points than any team in the league and forwards overall well under their averages. This is a structurally sound, middle-of-the-pack even-strength team. The record is not coming from what happens at full strength.

The damage is in three places. The penalty kill is at 69.1%, 29th, far below the league's 77.2%. The goalies are at -7.4 GSAx (26th), and Darcy Kuemper is carrying most of that: .885 and -4.8 in 13 starts, while Anton Forsberg (.901, -0.8) has been closer to neutral. Then there is a -3.4 Pts vs Goal Diff, 29th. The Kings have lost more than their share of the coin flips, including a six-game losing streak and a run of one-goal home losses in November. Last season was the mirror image: +5.6 in Pts vs Goal Diff propped a -0.27 goal-differential team up to 90 points. Both seasons look like noise around a team that is somewhere near average.

What the numbers hide is that the offense problem is real and not new. The Kings score 2.76 goals a game (26th, 0.44 below the league), and the offense ranked 29th last season too. The power play at 20.6% (22nd) isn't covering for it. Quinton Byfield is the bright spot. He has 6 goals on 48 shots and a 56.7% xGF while playing nearly 20 minutes, yet sits at -8, which is the season in miniature: good process, ugly results. The other worry is the arc. xGF % has slid from 55.2% two years ago to 52.4% last year to 50.4% now, so this is a fading good team, not a hidden contender.

Where it heads: some of the kill and the close-game luck should come back, and a team that controls play this evenly shouldn't keep losing at a 62-point pace. But the hole is real and the scoring ceiling is low. Expect a better second two-thirds than the first that still finishes well short of the playoff line unless the goaltending turns sharply.

strengths.title: Even-strength play holds up
strengths.body: At 5-on-5 the Kings are a break-even team: 50.4% of expected goals and 50.0% of shot attempts, both right at league average. That is a step down from prior years, but it is a sustainable baseline. It is not what a 29th-ranked team usually looks like, and it argues the record should improve.

strengths.title: Centers get shut down
strengths.body: No team holds opposing centers further under their usual production, and the Kings rank seventh against forwards overall. That points to sound middle-ice structure rather than goalie heroics, since the goalies have been below average. Positional suppression like this tends to persist when it shows up across 19 tracked games.

strengths.title: Byfield drives play
strengths.body: Byfield leads the listed forwards in ice time and shots and posts a 56.7% xGF. His -8 is a results problem, not a play problem, and those tend to even out as the goaltending behind him normalizes.

concerns.title: Penalty kill is bleeding goals
concerns.body: At 69.1% the kill is 29th and more than eight points below the league average. It was already slipping last season, at 74.6%. Some of this is goaltending, and some correction is likely. Still, a two-year decline suggests it won't snap back to the 81% of 2024-25.

concerns.title: Kuemper is underwater
concerns.body: The starter has a .885 save % and -4.8 GSAx in 13 starts, the bulk of the team's -7.4. The goaltending grade is a D. Forsberg has been better in a smaller sample, so the starts split is the lever to watch.

concerns.title: Scoring is a two-year problem
concerns.body: At 2.76 goals a game the offense is 26th, and it was 29th last season. The power play is below average as well. Unlike the kill and the goaltending, this doesn't look like bad luck. It looks like who this roster is.

trend.note: Flat and below water all season: a 4-8 October, a 3-5 November. The last 10 games (4-6-0) and last 5 (2-3-0) run at the same .400 points rate. Scoring has ticked up lately to 3.0 a game over the last 10, without changing the results.

weekAhead.headline: Lucky Montréal, then two with Anaheim's sieve
weekAhead.body:
The week opens in Montréal against a 14-6-4 team whose record runs well ahead of its play. The Canadiens lead the league in Pts vs Goal Diff (+3.4), carry a 102.1 PDO, and their 5-on-5 shares are about the same as LA's. Their real edge is in net (GSAx +11.5, 5th). Their 14.3% power play, 31st, is the rare unit LA's kill can handle. Montréal's defense also gives up more than expected to centers.

Then comes a home-and-home with Anaheim, which is a goaltending matchup the Kings should win. The Ducks' goalies have an .858 save % (last) and -10.7 GSAx (31st). Anaheim gets out-chanced at 5-on-5 (45.4% xGF, 27th) and lets opposing forwards, especially wingers, run well over their averages. The catch is the Ducks' power play, first in the league at 34.2%, against LA's 29th-ranked kill. Stay out of the box and these are games LA should take.

keyMatchups.title: Anaheim's PP vs LA's kill
keyMatchups.body: The league's best power play meets one of its worst penalty kills, twice in two days. This is the one way Anaheim can overcome being out-chanced at 5-on-5. Discipline decides the back-to-back.

keyMatchups.title: Byfield against Anaheim's wingers
keyMatchups.body: Anaheim is 29th at limiting wingers and 30th against forwards overall, and its goalies stop the fewest pucks in the league. A shooting winger driving play at Byfield's rate should find this a chance to turn process into points.

keyMatchups.title: Montréal's luck vs its goalies
keyMatchups.body: Montréal's record is propped up by close-game results and a hot PDO, but its goaltending is genuinely good. LA has to beat a +11.5 GSAx tandem at 5-on-5, because the Canadiens' power play won't hurt them.

weekAhead.watch: How many minor penalties LA takes against Anaheim's league-best power play.

restOfSeason.body:
The 62-point pace overstates how bad this team is. Even 5-on-5 shares, elite suppression of centers and a 29th-ranked Pts vs Goal Diff all point to better results. The kill and the goaltending have room to recover toward league norms, and close-game luck tends to even out. I'd expect the Kings to play near .500-ish hockey the rest of the way, which lands somewhere in the low-to-mid 70s in points.

What won't regress is the scoring. Two straight years near the bottom of the league in goals and a below-average power play cap the upside. The hole after 21 games is deep enough that even a solid stretch likely leaves them outside the playoff picture. The real question is whether this is a bad-luck season or the next step in a three-year slide in xGF %.
swingFactors: Kuemper's save % vs Forsberg's share of starts
Penalty kill recovering toward league average
Whether 5-on-5 play holds near 50% xGF or keeps sliding

confidence.note: 21 games is enough to trust the 5-on-5 shares, not the goalie and PK numbers.
